articles.headline: Nominating Convention.
articles.text:
Nominating Convention.

A convention of the citizens and qualified voters of Billings county, will be held Monday evening, March 1, 1886, to place in nomination a list of county officers to be voted for on the second Monday in April, 1886 and to hold office until the next regular fall election. A full attendance is requested.
articles.summary: Call for a Billings County nominating convention on March 1, 1886, to name candidates for the April county election.

articles.text: In some parts of Massachusetts, notably in Boston and Roxbury they are having destructive floods.
articles.summary: Brief note on floods in Boston and Roxbury, Massachusetts.

articles.text: One hundred and fifty delegates attended an anti-Chinese congress at Portland, Oregon, last Saturday. Although the feeling of the entire west is against the Chinese, the mob-law used in driving the Chinese out will lose the movement many friends.
articles.summary: Editorial comment on an anti-Chinese congress at Portland, Oregon.

articles.text: In another column will be found a communication written in answer to a letter making inquiries about alfalfa. From the answers, we see no reason why alfalfa should not be grown extensively in the Bad Lands, enough at least to make each cattleman independent of the native hay crop for ranch use. It is undoubtedly worth the trial.
articles.summary: The paper urges Bad Lands cattlemen to try growing alfalfa for hay.

articles.text: Lieut. J. M. T. Partello and wife of Ft. Keogh, returned from their European trip about a month ago. We notice in the last Western Rural, an article from the Lieutenant's gifted pen, describing the exciting experience of being chased by wolves. As before mentioned in the Cow Boy, the Lieutenant takes almost a corresponding rank among literery men that he does among marksmen.
articles.summary: Lt. J. M. T. Partello of Fort Keogh, back from Europe, wrote a Western Rural article on being chased by wolves.

articles.text: In view of the way horse-thieves are being cleaned out of the country and the almost absolute certainty of the capture of the thief and the recovery of the stock, it seems that a person must be either perfectly reckless or almost a fool to indulge in the pastime of running off another man's horses. Detection and capture are far more certain in the west than in the east and the punishment is more severe. Within the last two years especially, there has been good work done in clearing the country of these criminals or fools, and the good work is still going on so merrily that we can almost feel the time when horse-stealing will become a lost art. We have not heard of a white man's horse being stolen west of the Missouri in Dakota, for nearly a year.
articles.summary: Editorial says horse-stealing west of the Missouri has nearly been stamped out.

articles.text: Several Billings county tax-payers have paid their taxes to Stark county. The vast majority, however, remain unpaid. To avoid difficulty, we advise by all means that an injunction be issued on the treasurer of Stark county, enjoining him from collecting the tax until the constitutionality of the law can be passed upon. There is no doubt whatever that at least part of the tax is uncollectable and a test case will show the unconstitutionality of the whole law. As the matter stands at present, the treasurer of Stark county has authority to compel payment of taxes, together with his fees and mileage which will amount to over $80 for each trip.
articles.summary: The paper urges an injunction against Stark County collecting taxes from Billings County residents.

articles.headline: Alfalfa.
articles.text:
Alfalfa.

Denver, Colorado, Feb. 9, 1886.

A. T. Packard,

Dear Sir:—

Your favor of Jan. 30, to Mr. J. W. Hill, Las Vegas, was sent to us by that gentleman for reply as there is no Alfalfa seed raised in N. M. That territory is supplied by Utah and Colorado. Now we will answer your questions.

1. Alfalfa will grow on dry land without irrigating, but will not yield as heavy as when irrigated.

2. It will yield perhaps three to four tons of hay per acre.

3. It will furnish two cuttings of one and a half to two tons each, and should be cut when it just comes in bloom.

4. It is a perennial clover and will last a life time without reseeding.

5. We are not positive whether it will stand such severe frosts as fifty degrees below zero but feel convinced that it will, as it is the hardiest of the clover family.

6. It requires about twenty-five to thirty lbs to sow one acre of ground, it can be sown either broadcast or with a drill, in the latter case it is advisable to drill it both lengthways and crossways to procure an even stand.

7. Best quality of seed is selling at $14 per 100 lbs. It weighs sixty lbs. to the bushel.

8. The cutting, baling etc. is the same as with Red Clover.

9. Alfalfa hay is in every respect superior to Red Clover or Timothy hay as to fattening qualities.

10. It is sowed and cut like other hay.

11. It will grow if sown on sod, but the ground should be loosened a little, and after seeding, well harrowed, thus preventing the seed from being blown away. However, we recommend to sow it on plowed ground.

12. It thrives best on a sandy, loam soil. Wet underground is fatal to the plant. The proper time for sowing is about April 1. Any further information will be cheerfully given.

Yours Truly,

Barteldes & Patch.
articles.summary: Denver seedsmen Barteldes & Patch answer Packard's questions about growing alfalfa in the Bad Lands.

articles.text: The spring meeting of the Montana Stockgrowers' association begins at Miles City, April 19.
articles.summary: Montana Stockgrowers' Association spring meeting set for Miles City, April 19.

articles.text: At least a week before the meeting in Miles City, there should be a meeting of the Little Missouri river association, to arrange for the round-up and other matters of general interest. The time above all others then for holding this meeting is April 12, the day of the election for county officers. The reason for this is too manifest to need any urging. It will be an additional incentive for every cowman especially to be in attendance at the election and a far larger vote will be polled than would be possible if some other day were set for the meeting. We hope the officer issuing the call will bear this fact in mind.
articles.summary: The paper urges the Little Missouri River stockmen's association to meet April 12, election day, to plan the round-up.

articles.text: We have received several inquiries as to the per cent. of loss among cattle in the Bad Lands. To one familiar with the range cattle business, it is manifest that a definite answer to this question is an utter impossibility. It is certainly less than it was last year when the highest estimate of loss was three per cent. Cattle entered on this winter in much poorer condition than they were at a corresponding time the previous year, but we have had less real winter weather so far than we had in any month of last winter. Cattle have fully or more than held their own and it must be severe weather that will make much of a loss.
articles.summary: The paper estimates Bad Lands winter cattle losses as lower than last year's three per cent, citing a mild winter.

articles.text:
Heavy losses of cattle occurred in Kansas, Wyoming, Montana, Dakota and other states during the recent terrible blizzard. Many have been found frozen to death standing on their feet. Colorado and New Mexico have suffered comparatively little, while Arizona had no loss to speak of. In many cases of death, the cause may be attributed to cattle drifting against wire fences.—[Arizona Hoof and Horn.

Outside of the remarkable fact that the frame-work of the above article has appeared in nearly every one of our cattle exchanges extending from the Gulf of Mexico to Canada, with appropriate changes in making its own state or territory most free from loss and outsiders suffering terribly, there is nothing in the above article but pure "filling." There has been no genuine blizzard in either Dakota or Montana this year and "the recent terrible blizzard" alluded to, came no nearer us than Colorado and at that very time, we were having the pleasantest weather we have had this winter. We might add that we never saw or heard of a wire fence either in Dakota or Montana that was long enough to harm cattle in any way. Such articles, aside from the absolute untruth of their statements, throw discredit on all its articles in particular and the entire range press in general. There is too great a tendency among cattle papers to exaggerate and it is time to call a halt.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy rebuts an Arizona Hoof and Horn item, saying Dakota and Montana have had no genuine blizzard this winter.

articles.headline: Nine-tenths Bogus.
articles.text:
Nine-tenths Bogus.

We asked an extensive and fashionable grocer of this city a few day's since what proportion of the product sold in Chicago as butter was butterine. He replied without hesitation: Nine-tenths! Nine-tenths of the stuff sold as butter is not butter. We asked him if he sold it? He replied: Not intentionally, but I presume I do for it is impossible to tell it from butter unless one is an expert. Here is plenty of food for thought, without stopping to consider whether or not the grocer told the truth when he said he did not intentionally sell it. It is not very clear from what he said that he believed nine-tenths of what he sold for butter was butterine. It is very clear that he did not care if it was, and therefore, if he knew what it was he purposely bought it to impose upon his customers; and if he did not know what it was then he was imposed upon by somebody else. In either case the stuff is being sold as butter, a rank fraud. Now what is to be said about such a state of things? Is it not incredible that people will submit to being swindled in this way and to this extent? Is it not incredible that butter-makers will submit to such an injustice when it is within their power to compel legislatures and law-officers to protect them? And yet, notwithstanding that nine-tenths of the butter sold in Chicago is nothing but an imitation, we are told over and over again that bogus butters do not hurt the sales of genuine butter if it is good butter. Suppose this nine-tenths of imitation butter was not made, does it require any argument to show that pure butter must be had to supply the deficiency, and if there was not enough to supply it that the price of butter would quickly rise.

According to the statement of this grocer, nine-tenths of the people of this city are eating bogus butter. Yet at the very time he was telling us this, creamery butter was worth in this city forty cents a pound, at retail, and this bogus stuff was being sold as creamery butter at that price. If the imitations had not been filling the market is it unreasonable to suppose that creamery butter would have been much higher than forty cents? A little common sense in the matter is quite as good as figures.—[Western Rural.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Western Rural on imitation butter sold as butter in Chicago.

articles.headline: Overstocking the Range.
articles.text:
Overstocking the Range.

Let me warn the amateur cowman that in the great grazing regions it takes a great many acres of thin grass to maintain the adult steer in affluence for twelve months, and the great pastures at the base of the mountains are being pretty well tested. Moreover, I believe that these great conventions of cattlemen, where free grass and easily acquired fortunes are naturally advertised, will tend to over-stock the ranges at last, and founder the goose that now lays the golden egg. This, of course, is none of my business, but if I didn't now and then refer to matters that don't concern me I would be regarded as reticent.—[Bill Nye.
articles.summary: Bill Nye warns that cattlemen's conventions advertising free grass will overstock the range.

articles.text: No distinct breed of horses, it is thought, had its origin in this country. The broncho or mustang is a peculiar type of horse, but it is a sort of uncivilized descendant of the horses brought over by the first Spanish settlers of this country, crossed with other breeds which have escaped from civilization, perhaps during the early wars. These little horses, though, have bred and raised their young of the same peculiar type so long, perhaps for over a century, and their traits are so distinct and well established that they may now be considered a distinct breed, peculiar only to the western and southwestern plains of America. These horses may now not only be considered a well established breed, but they have many excellent qualities which might be engrafted upon the breeds in common use with evident advantage. These qualities are their proverbial hardiness, toughness and powers of endurance. Perhaps no other breed posesses these most desirable qualities in a horse in a greater or even in an equal degree, and it is very desirable that they be perpetuated in a larger and more [useful?] [illegible] by crossing the mustang mares with stallions of the large breeds.—[N. M. Stock Grower.
articles.summary: Reprint from the N. M. Stock Grower on the broncho or mustang as a distinct breed worth crossing with larger stock.

articles.headline: The Arabian Horse.
articles.text:
The Arabian Horse.

The Arabians profess to trace the ancestry of their horses back to the time of Solomon, yet in the light of authentic history, their horses before the Thirteenth century were not of a character worthy of special notice. The horse of the desert receives the personal care and affection of his master. To the Arab the horse is not only a companion in solitude, but is also his only means of locomotion in arduous and perilous journeys. It is not strange, therefore, that these nomads of the desert should bestow much care upon the breeding and rearing of their horses; and during the past seven centuries such care has been bestowed. The Arabs did undoutedly understand the true principle of breeding, care, feeding, selection and training, at a period when Arabia was the seat of learning and all Europe was enveloped in the gloom of the dark ages, or was just beginning feebly to see the dawn of the revival of letters.

Arabian travellers of the last century do not agree as to the number of distinct breeds of horses in that country. A Mohammedan writer who seems to have had candor, and a good opportunity for gathering facts, divides them into six tribes, as follows:

The Dgelfe, found chiefly in Arabia Felix, seldom seen in Damascus, but common in Anaze. Horses of this breed are of lofty stature, have narrow chests, but are deep in the girth, and their ears are long. They are remarkable for spirit and fleetness, but are extremely tractable, and their ability to endure hunger and thirst is a remarkable feature.

The Secaloni, a breed from the eastern part of the desert, somewhat inferior to the Dgelfe, though resembling him in most points.

The Mefki, is a handsome horse, but not so fleet as either the Dgelfe or the Secaloni. In figure he has the resemblance to the Spanish or Andalusian stock.

A fourth breed is called the Sabi, similar to the Mefki but seems to posess no specially useful or striking qualities.

The Fridi. This breed is very common, but they are often vicious and untrustworthy, and lack some of the excellent qualities posessed by the best of the others.

The Nejdi, found chiefly in the region of Bussorah. These are said to be at least the equals of the Dgelfe and the Secaloni. Some judges assert there is no horse to be compared with them, and they stand very high in the market. The Dgelfe and Nejdi are reported to be the most valuable. They are known to be the favorites of the horse fanciers of India, many fine animals of these stocks have been carried thither by the sportsmen of that country.—[Pictorial L. S. Cyclopedia.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Pictorial L. S. Cyclopedia describing six Arabian horse breeds.

articles.text: Relying on an authority we suppposed to be good, the Cow Boy of two weeks ago contained a statement to the effect that W. H. Merrifield had taken unto himself a wife on his eastern trip. On his return, we found that our informant, laboring under the delusion that it was funny, had made up the story out of whole cloth. This is as far from our idea of fun as black is from white and we cannot appreciate the sentiments of anyone who can even see a funny side to it.
articles.summary: The paper retracted its report that W. H. Merrifield had married on his eastern trip.

articles.text: "Calamity Joe" was captured last Saturday at Glenullin, by Sheriff Sebastian and Deputy Goudy, of Stark county. He came in from Rapid City to Glenullin, when word was immediately sent to the Stark county officers. He was found in the post-office and on seeing the officers, started to escape, running through the back door. The officers ordered him to stop but he refused to obey. As he was armed with an ugly looking six-shooter, the officers were compelled to fire on him, bringing him down with wounds in the left side and fleshy par of the hip, the shot in the side breaking a rib, but neither wound being serious. On receiving the wounds he dropped and attempted to return the fire, but his revolver refused to work and he wisely gave himself up. He was taken to Dickinson, where he will lie in jail until he is able to undergo his preliminary examination; probably in a week or ten days. It is amusing to read in eastern papers that he was one of the most notorious desperadoes and horse-thieves in the entire west. He was known here as a quiet, peaceable man, perhaps a trifle weak in the upper story, but with nothing of the criminal about him naturally. This weakness is shown by his coming back to the scene of his crime, where everyone knew him, when he knew that officers were searching everywhere for him. If it had not been for his intimacy with horse-thieves, we doubt if he would ever have stolen a horse.
articles.summary: "Calamity Joe" was shot and captured at Glenullin by Stark county officers and jailed at Dickinson.

articles.headline: Notice of Election.
articles.text:
Notice of Election.

Notice is hereby given that on the Second (2nd.) Monday in April, 1886, at the following place, viz.: at the town of

Medora,

in the County of Billings, an election will be held for the following officers of said county of Billings, in said Territory of Dakota, in the organization of said county;

Three County Commissioners,
One Register of Deeds,
One County Clerk,
One Sheriff,
One Assessor,
One Judge of Probate,
One County Treasurer,
One County Surveyor,
One Coroner,
One Superintendent of Public Schools,
Four Justices of the Peace,
Four Constables,
and also for the temporary location of the County seat of said county,

which election will be open at the hour of eight o'clock in the morning and will continue open until five o'clock in the afternoon of the same day.

Dated this 20th. day of January, 1886.

{Seal.} Gilbert A. Pierce, Governor.

M. L. McCormack, Secretary.
articles.summary: Governor Pierce's notice of the election to organize Billings County, to be held at Medora on the second Monday in April 1886.
